Photograph: Photographer, Basak Gurbuz Derman/Getty Images Heart attack Drones could speed up getting defibrillators to people having cardiac arrests, study suggests New research suggests the technology could be used to increase out-of-hospital access to life-saving devices Nicola Davis Science correspondent Sat 26 Sep 2026 01.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Drones could help cut the time it takes to get a defibrillator to people experiencing cardiac arrests when not in hospital, researchers have suggested. In the UK alone, there are more than 30,000 out-of-hospital cardiac arrests a year where emergency medical services attempt to resuscitate the individual, according to the British Heart Foundation. However, fewer than one in 10 people survive such an event, and some who do are left with neurological problems. One important factor that can affect survival is how rapidly victims get access to treatment – every minute without CPR and defibrillation reduces the chance of survival by 10% . “We have an objective as EMS [emergency medical service] organisations and EMS physicians to help cardiac arrest patients get defibrillated as early as possible,” said Matthieu Heidet, a professor of emergency medicine at Henri-Mondor university hospital in Créteil, France . Work by Heidet and colleagues has suggested drones could be used to increase access to the life-saving devices. To explore the issue, the team analysed the number and location of 28,349 out-of-hospital cardiac arrests that occurred between 2011 and 2024 in administrative areas within the Greater Paris area. Central Paris was excluded from the analysis. The team cross-referenced these events with the location of fixed automated external defibrillators (AEDs). The researchers found accessibility of the 1,893 AEDs varied considerably across the area. “Only 30% of all [out-of-hospital cardiac arrest] cases occurred within the target 500-metre network distance of the nearest recorded fixed AED,” said Dr Hillary Minka, an emergency physician at the Lariboisière hospital in Paris and the first author of the work. The team found an extra 910 fixed AEDs would be needed for 84.5% of the recorded cardiac arrest cases to have been within 500 metres of an AED, while 1,712 extra fixed AEDs would be needed for 100% coverage. However, by using drones operating within a radius of 3,900 metres, coverage could be increased with fewer devices. “As drone bases were introduced, the number of additional fixed AEDs required fell substantially,” said Minka, noting that with 100 drone bases and 26 additional fixed AEDs, more than 97% of the cardiac arrest cases would have been located either within 500 metres of a fixed AED or within approximately 4km (2.5 miles) of a drone base. The use of 200 drone bases and just four extra AEDs meant more than 99% of cases would have been covered. The researchers also looked at the proportion of the cardiac arrest cases deemed close enough to an existing fixed AED that the device could be retrieved in a round trip within five minutes. The results revealed only 30-40% of the cardiac arrest cases had access to current fixed AEDs within this time period using the ground transportation network. Heidet added that this figure was optimistic. “In France, only 8% of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest patients benefit from the application of a public AED before the arrival of the [emergency services],” he said, noting one factor is that a large proportion of AEDs are inaccessible , for example because they are housed in enclosed private spaces that are not open at all times. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion By contrast, Minka noted that in a scenario involving 200 drone bases, 871 existing fixed AED sites and four additional fixed AED sites, drone delivery reached virtually all of the cardiac arrest cases covered by the model within five minutes. The team’s models were based on drones being housed at sites ranging from current AED locations to fire stations and mobile intensive care units, and did not look at real-world deployment of such tech. Heidet noted it is not the first time drones have been considered for the delivery of AEDs; the approach is already being used in parts of Sweden and has saved lives . In real-world systems, Heidet added, drones are operated by trained drone pilots. More than 16m at risk of death by cardiac arrest in England and Wales due to ‘defibrillator deserts’ Read more “Once an emergency call is received and an [out-of-hospital cardiac arrest] is identified at the dispatch centre, the drone is activated by EMS dispatchers. It then takes off and follows an automated flight path, while the final approach and subsequent AED delivery are handled by the drone pilot. The entire process is conducted under the supervision of the emergency medical service,” he said. Once delivered, the AED can be used by members of the public at the scene. Heidet added the cost of drones needed to be integrated into the evaluation of such technology, noting there may be a balance between the ideal model and the feasible economic model. The study, which has not yet been peer-reviewed, is to be presented at the European Emergency Medicine Congress in Paris on Saturday. https://www.politico.eu/article/france-c.text: Eleven defendants will face trial in France after being accused of killing a 16-year-old in 2023 while engaging in speech “against the white race and the French nation,” according to a judicial order seen by POLITICO. The death of Thomas Perotto in the village of Cr´epol quickly became a political flashpoint, with far-right figures like Eric Zemmour framing the incident as an example of the threat posed by immigrants. President Emmanuel Macron called it a “terrible assassination,” while far-right leader Marine Le Pen described the attack as the work of an “armed militia.” Advertisement Advertisement The killing later fueled far-right mobilization , including an attempted “punitive expedition” by identitarian militants in nearby Romans-sur-Isère. French judges have sent 11 defendants to the juvenile assize court over the 2023 stabbing to death of 16-year-old Thomas Perotto, with the case involving a racial aggravating factor in the reference to “the white race and the French nation,” French media reported Friday. The order sending them to trial, seen by POLITICO, accuses the defendants of murdering Perotto at a village fête in Crépol, attempting to kill three other people and violently attacking others. Judges seek to trial them as a group because the investigation hasn’t determined who is alleged to have delivered the fatal blow, AFP reported . The judges’ order states the alleged killing was “preceded, accompanied or followed by words, writings, images, objects or acts of any kind” harming the honor of victims or a group because of their supposed race, ethnicity, nation or religion — “in this case, the white race and the French nation.” Some defendants were minors when the attack took place. All are presumed innocent. The Valence prosecutor’s office had initially sought trial on murder and attempted murder charges without the aggravating factor, saying witness statements supporting it were “in the minority” and “imprecise.” Denis Dreyfus, a lawyer representing a group of attendees claiming damages, told POLITICO that the charges matched arguments his side had made. “We welcome the considerable work carried out by the investigating judges,” he said, adding that the case should now proceed with “the dignity due to Thomas and the victims.” The defense pushed back on the charges. “How can our client be sent to trial for murder aggravated by a racial circumstance when neither the fatal blow nor any racist remarks are personally attributed to him?” lawyers Seydi Ba and Diala Al-Shaman, who represent one of the defendants, said, according to AFP . A trial date has not been set. Elise Rey-Jacquot, a lawyer representing another defendent, told RTL on Saturday she would appeal the charges, potentially delaying proceedings.
